text: I’ll model the cavity in metres, centred at the shaft-axis intersection. The pinion axis will run toward the +X wall and the wheel axis toward the +Z wall. Because face width and shaft size were not specified, I’ll initially assume an 18 mm face width and 16 mm shaft/bore diameter; both shafts stop at the gear backs and continue to their respective walls. The bevel pitch-cone angles will come from the 20:30 tooth ratio at a 90° shaft angle. I’ll generate straight, tapered teeth from explicit pressure-angle flank geometry, subtract both geared shaft solids from the box, export conformal patch STLs, and use snappyHexMesh coarse-first. First I’m checking the installed CAD API needed for lofting and face selection.

The API supports direct ruled lofts. I’ll now build one representative pinion tooth in a local shaft coordinate system and verify its dimensions before replicating it. This isolates the pressure-angle construction from the later gear boolean operations.

The first loft attempt exposed an API mismatch: `Polygon` already returns a planar face-like sketch, so wrapping it in `Face` produced an empty shape. I’ll correct that constructor and repeat only this tooth test.
I’ll re-emit the corrected tooth test with every required parameter defined in the accepted cell so the final `build.py` remains reproducible from empty.

The single-tooth measurements match the requested module, pressure angle, and the allocated half-backlash. I’ll now replicate the teeth, add tapered root bodies and the assumed 16 mm shafts, orient the axes at 90°, and test the mating phase by measuring any solid overlap. The wheel is phased half a tooth pitch so a pinion tooth faces a wheel space at the common pitch line.

The centred phase still has an 11.3 mm³ interference, so the linear-flank approximation is not conjugate enough even though its pitch-point angle is correct. I will replace only the transverse tooth outline with a sampled involute generated from the 20° base circle; the taper along the cone remains straight. This should preserve the specified pitch-line backlash while removing off-pitch flank interference.

The involute reduced interference by about 70% but did not eliminate it. I’ll inspect the interference location before changing geometry; if it is confined to tooth tips away from the pitch line, I can add local tip/root clearance without altering the measured 0.3 mm pitch-line backlash.

The remaining overlap is one narrow mating-flank sliver (3.58 mm³) across the face, not a shaft or hub collision. I’ll inspect the installed solid-offset operation so I can apply a very small local running clearance to that sliver while retaining the explicitly measured 0.3 mm pitch-line tooth-space allocation.

Before adding a relief, I’ll test the standard manufacturing convention of putting all 0.3 mm backlash reduction on the wheel while leaving the pinion at nominal thickness. The total pitch-line gap remains exactly 0.3 mm, but the off-pitch involute geometry can differ enough to remove this small residual interference.

Redistributing backlash did not remove the sliver. I’ll therefore add 0.10 mm of symmetric off-pitch flank relief per gear, ramped to exactly zero at the pitch radius. This is a chosen manufacturing-clearance assumption: it leaves the requested pitch-line backlash unchanged at 0.300 mm while preventing the approximate straight-bevel tooth surfaces from intersecting away from the pitch point.

The relief barely changed the overlap, indicating the collision is likely between a tooth tip and the opposite root cone rather than between active flanks. I’ll separate those intersections numerically before deciding the correct tip/root clearance change.

The collision is entirely pinion-tip versus wheel-root; the root cones do not intersect. Since the request did not specify an addendum system, I’ll replace my initial full-depth 1.0-module addendum assumption with a short 0.8-module addendum on both gears, retaining the 1.25-module dedendum and the exact pitch geometry. This provides a larger tip path while preserving tooth count, module, pressure angle, and pitch-line backlash.

The final gear solids are now non-intersecting. I’m moving directly to the coarse mesh: first I’ll cut the cavity and classify its boundary faces by their generating solids—box, pinion/wheel, or the two shaft cylinders—then export all five conformal patch STLs in one call.
